text: {"lesson":{"schemaVersion":1,"title":"Lesson F4: Flex Day: Meaning-Making Huddle/Catch-Up Day","lessonType":"flex-day","header":{"focusStandards":[],"supportingStandards":[],"eldStandards":[],"mediaLiteracyStandards":[],"objectives":[{"kind":"content","text":"Students will revisit sections of The Lightning Thief that need more time, citing specific details to explain what happens, how figurative language shapes tone, and how Percy's choices develop theme."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will explain their thinking about the novel aloud and in writing using evidence-introducing phrases such as 'In Chapter 14, the text says...' and 'This shows that...'."},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will reread a short passage aloud with accuracy and expression to build meaning before explaining it."}],"essentialQuestions":["How do authors retell ancient myths in modern ways, and what do those retellings teach us?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"Students deepen their understanding of Riordan's modern retelling of Greek myth by revisiting chapters from Investigation 2 (Chapters 13, 14, 19, 20 and 22) where they most need support.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from different cultures and times show what people value, how they explain the world, and what it means to be human. Close rereading helps us see that.","futureLessons":"Next, students plan the Shared Stories, Shared Lessons essay. Solid understanding of the novel's key moments, details and themes gives them evidence to draw on when comparing myths.","performanceTask":"The performance task asks students to explain what myths teach us, using evidence from several texts. Today students strengthen their command of The Lightning Thief evidence and meaning so they can use it in that essay."}, "vocabulary":[{"word":"evidence","definition":"a specific detail or quotation from the text that supports an idea","tier":"support"},{"word":"figurative language","definition":"words used in a non-literal way, such as similes and exaggeration, to create an effect","tier":"support"},{"word":"tone","definition":"the author's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice","tier":"support"},{"word":"theme","definition":"a message or big idea about life that a story develops","tier":"support"},{"word":"turning point","definition":"a moment in a story when something important changes","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Teacher's choice of: Chapter 13 (Gateway Arch battle); Chapter 14 (the river); Chapter 19, pp. 300-309 (Fields of Asphodel); Chapter 20, pp. 327-333 (Percy and Ares); Chapter 22, pp. 354-369"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students quickly rate which parts of the novel feel least clear so the teacher can form responsive huddles.","activities":[{"id":"launch-confidence-check","title":"Where Do I Need Another Look?","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Rate each statement from 1 (not yet) to 4 (I can teach it). Write your three numbers on a sticky note or on your whiteboard. 1) I can use details from the story to prove that Percy is a child of a god (Chapter 14). 2) I can explain how Riordan's figurative language creates tone (Chapters 13 and 19). 3) I can explain how Percy's choices show a theme (Chapters 20 and 22)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today is a catch-up day. We will go back into The Lightning Thief to make sure the big moments make sense. Rate yourself honestly, because your ratings and your recent work will decide which huddle you join."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which chapter would you most like another look at, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I want to look at Chapter 19 again because the Fields of Asphodel was confusing. I didn't get why people just stood around and why that was scary."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Sort students using ratings plus recent work: reading responses, Unit Vocabulary organizers, and thematic summaries. You do not need all three huddles. Swap in any chapter your class finds hardest. Students not in a huddle work on the Independent Choice Work listed in each huddle."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Three targeted small-group huddles revisit sections of The Lightning Thief that students need more time with, while other students work independently.","activities":[{"id":"huddle-1-evidence-turning-point","title":"Huddle 1: Evidence and Turning Points (Chapter 14)","minutes":13,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who rated 1-2 on statement 1, or whose recent responses name an idea (for example, 'Percy is special') without a specific detail from the text. Others begin Independent Choice Work."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Independent Choice Work (choose one). Option 1: Reread any page of your independent reading book and write one sentence about a character, then add one detail that supports it. Option 2: Reread your Unit Vocabulary organizer and write two sentences about the novel using two vocabulary words from Lessons 20-22."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 14","pages":"The river sequence: Percy staying dry, breathing underwater, and lighting a lighter at the bottom of the river"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Reteach: **Evidence** is a specific detail or quote from the text. A **turning point** is a moment when the story changes direction. In Chapter 14 the fall, the underwater sequence and the emergence together form a turning point that raises the stakes of the quest and echoes a death-and-rebirth pattern."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Strong thinking has two parts: an idea and a detail that proves it. 'Percy is special' is an idea. 'Percy lights a lighter at the bottom of the river' is a detail. Our job is to connect them."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Reread the underwater scene. What specific details show that Percy is a child of a god?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy stays dry in the water, he can breathe underwater, and he even lights a lighter at the bottom of the river. A normal person couldn't do any of those things."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why is this a turning point in the story? What changes between the fall and the emergence?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Before, Percy wasn't sure about his powers. After he comes up out of the river, everyone has seen what he can do, so the quest feels more serious. It's like he went down and came back up changed, like a rebirth."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Quick Check: write two sentences. First an idea about Percy, then a detail from Chapter 14 using the frame 'In Chapter 14, the text shows... This proves that...'."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's powers are connected to water. In Chapter 14, the text shows that he stays dry and breathes underwater at the bottom of the river. This proves that he is a child of a god."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":[],"stem":"In Chapter 14, which detail from the river sequence best supports the idea that Percy is a child of a god?","choices":[{"text":"Percy stays dry, breathes underwater, and lights a lighter at the bottom of the river.","correct":true,"rationale":"These impossible details are concrete evidence of divine parentage."},{"text":"Percy falls from a high place during the battle.","correct":false,"rationale":"The fall starts the sequence, but anyone could fall, so it does not prove he is special."},{"text":"Percy is tired and wants to rest after the fight.","correct":false,"rationale":"Being tired shows nothing about divine parentage."},{"text":"Percy talks with the other heroes about the quest.","correct":false,"rationale":"Talking about the quest is plot, not evidence of his parentage."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners move from a general idea to a specific, text-based detail and explain the connection.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the exact line first, then say your idea. Frames: 'One detail is...' 'This shows that...' 'The turning point is when...'. Recast: You said 'he is magic' - we can say 'The text shows he can breathe underwater, so he is a child of a god.' Let students tell a partner in their home language first, then in English.","watchFor":"If a student gives an idea with no detail, then ask 'Which line shows that?' If a student copies a detail without explaining it, then prompt 'This shows that...'. Success: the student names a specific Chapter 14 detail and links it to Percy's identity."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding a specific detail","tryThis":"Give a short list of three events from the river scene and have the student circle the one that shows Percy is not ordinary. Then reread that page aloud together."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the death-and-rebirth pattern of the fall, underwater sequence and emergence connects to an older myth hero they have read."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-2-figurative-tone","title":"Huddle 2: Figurative Language and Tone (Chapters 13 and 19)","minutes":13,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who rated 1-2 on statement 2, or who define figurative language but cannot say what effect it creates. Others do Independent Choice Work."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Independent Choice Work (choose one). Option 1: Find one simile or comparison in your independent reading and explain what it helps you picture. Option 2: Write two sentences using two of these words correctly: spectacle, apathy, eternal, vicious."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 13 and Chapter 19","pages":"Chapter 13: the Chimera battle at the Gateway Arch (the 'huge shopping bag handle'); Chapter 19, pp. 300-309: the Fields of Asphodel"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Reteach: **Figurative language** says one thing to mean another, such as a comparison. **Tone** is the attitude the words create. In Chapter 13 Riordan modernizes a classic hero-versus-monster fight with a modern setting and humor. In Chapter 19 his comparisons build a hollow mood of endless waiting, where apathy is a different kind of danger than a monster."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In Chapter 13, the Gateway Arch gets compared to a 'huge shopping bag handle.' What does this comparison do to the battle's tone?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It makes a serious monster fight sound funny and ordinary. A shopping bag handle is an everyday thing, so the tone is humorous even though the stakes are high."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Now look at pp. 300-309. What details, like the concert that never starts or stalactites compared to booster rockets, show the mood of the Fields of Asphodel?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The concert that never starts shows people waiting forever with nothing happening. The booster rockets comparison makes the cave feel like a modern thing that will never launch. Together the mood feels empty and hopeless, a danger of not caring instead of a monster."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Quick Check: pick one comparison from either chapter. Write: 'Riordan compares... to... This creates a ___ tone because...'."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Riordan compares the Gateway Arch to a huge shopping bag handle. This creates a humorous tone because it makes a dangerous fight feel everyday and silly."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":[],"stem":"In Chapter 19, what mood do details like the concert that never starts help create in the Fields of Asphodel?","choices":[{"text":"A hollow mood of endless waiting where nothing ever happens.","correct":true,"rationale":"The concert that never begins shows people stuck waiting forever, which creates an empty mood."},{"text":"An excited mood because a big show is about to begin.","correct":false,"rationale":"A concert sounds exciting, but it never actually starts, so the excitement never arrives."},{"text":"A frightening mood because a monster is chasing Percy.","correct":false,"rationale":"The danger in this section is apathy, not a chasing monster."},{"text":"A peaceful mood because the souls are enjoying themselves.","correct":false,"rationale":"The souls are not enjoying anything; they are bored and stuck."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in naming the effect of a comparison, not only spotting it.","sayAsk":"Say: First say what the two things are, then say how it feels. Frames: 'Riordan compares ___ to ___.' 'This makes the tone feel ___.' 'The mood is ___ because...'. Recast: You said 'it is funny' - we can say 'The comparison creates a humorous tone.' Offer a word bank: humorous, hollow, hopeless, everyday.","watchFor":"If a student only names the comparison, then ask 'How does it make the scene feel?' If a student confuses tone and mood, then say 'Tone is the author's attitude; mood is how the reader feels.' Success: the student names the comparison and its effect."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: explaining effect","tryThis":"Offer a choice of three tone words (humorous, serious, gloomy) and ask which fits the comparison and why before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite the shopping bag handle sentence in a serious tone and explain how the tone changes."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-3-theme-resolution","title":"Huddle 3: Theme and Resolution (Chapters 20 and 22)","minutes":14,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who rated 1-2 on statement 3, or whose summaries mix in opinion or retell events without naming a theme. Others do Independent Choice Work."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Independent Choice Work (choose one). Option 1: Write a three-sentence summary of Chapter 20, pp. 327-333, including buildup, confrontation and outcome. Option 2: Write a sentence explaining how one character in your independent reading changes from beginning to end."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 20 and Chapter 22","pages":"Chapter 20, pp. 327-333 (Percy and Ares); Chapter 22, pp. 354-369 (Percy's choice about home)"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Reteach: a **theme** is a message about life, not a topic. 'Home' is a topic; 'Home can be the place where you choose to belong' is a theme. A text-based summary tells what happened and how the theme develops, with no 'I think' opinions. Chapter 20 pp. 327-333 maps buildup, confrontation and outcome with Ares. Chapter 22 develops home, choice and identity through Percy's decisions."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Map the Ares fight in pp. 327-333. What are the buildup, the confrontation and the outcome?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The buildup is Percy facing Ares who is angry and powerful. The confrontation is the fight, where Percy gets hurt and takes risks. The outcome is that the conflict with Ares is resolved and Percy has grown braver."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In Chapter 22, how do Percy's choices show a theme about home or identity?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy has to decide where he belongs, and he chooses Camp Half-Blood. That shows that home is something you choose, and that he is accepting who he is as a demigod."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Quick Check: write a two-sentence summary. Start with the event, then state the theme. Frame: 'In Chapter 22, Percy... This develops the theme that...'. No 'I think'."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 22, Percy decides to return to Camp Half-Blood. This develops the theme that home is the place where you choose to belong."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":[],"stem":"Which sentence is a theme, not just a topic or an event, for Chapter 22?","choices":[{"text":"Home is where you choose to belong.","correct":true,"rationale":"It is a message about life that Percy's choice develops."},{"text":"Home.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is only a topic word; it does not say anything about it."},{"text":"Percy decides to return to Camp Half-Blood.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is an event, not a message about life."},{"text":"I think the ending is great.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is an opinion, not a text-based theme."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners separate topic, event and theme, and write a summary without opinion.","sayAsk":"Say: Event first, then message. Frames: 'First, Percy ___.' 'This shows the theme that ___.' 'The outcome is ___.' Recast: You said 'the theme is home' - we can say 'The theme is that home is where you choose to belong.' Use a three-box graphic organizer: buildup, confrontation, outcome.","watchFor":"If a student writes a one-word theme, then ask 'What does the story say about it?' If a student writes 'I think', then ask 'What does the text show?' Success: a two-sentence summary with an event and a complete theme statement."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: stating a theme","tryThis":"Provide the frame 'The story shows that ___ can ___' and a topic bank (home, choice, trust, sacrifice). Help students pick one and finish the sentence from a detail."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to connect Percy's idea of home to Odysseus's in Odyssey Book 13 and note one similarity and one difference, as preparation for the performance task."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on what became clearer and name one idea or detail they will carry into the performance task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"One Thing That Clicked","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Option A (huddle students): Re-rate yourself on the statement you worked on. What changed? Option B (independent students): Write one detail from your work today and what it shows about the story. Use the frame 'Today I understood... because the text says...'."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one detail from The Lightning Thief that you could use as evidence when you write about myths next time?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I could use the detail where Percy breathes underwater in Chapter 14, because it shows how Riordan keeps the idea of heroes with divine parents but puts it in a modern story."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Invite two or three students to share. Note who still rates 1-2 and plan to check in with them during the next planning lesson."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Flex Day offering three small-group huddles that revisit Chapters 13, 14, 19, 20 and 22 of The Lightning Thief: using specific evidence and turning points, explaining figurative language and tone, and stating theme and resolution in text-based summaries. Students rate their confidence, join a huddle by need, and reflect on one detail to carry into the Shared Stories, Shared Lessons performance task.","keyActivities":["Launch confidence check to sort students into huddles","Huddle 1: evidence and turning point in Chapter 14's river sequence","Huddle 2: figurative language and tone in Chapters 13 and 19","Huddle 3: theme and resolution in Chapters 20 and 22","Look Back quick write"],"vocabularyTaught":["evidence","figurative language","tone","theme","turning point"],"standardsCovered":[]}}
